nameStory: This lichen gets its 'red-cored starburst' name from the striking crimson center that shows through when you break open its fruiting bodies, creating a dramatic color contrast against the grayish exterior. The 'shadow' part of its name reflects how these crusty lichens seem to lurk quietly in the shadows of tree bark, easily overlooked until you know what to look for.
description: Red-cored Starburst Shadow Lichen is a crusty, gray-green lichen that forms small, circular patches on tree bark. Like all lichens, it's actually two organisms living together - a fungus and an algae working as partners to survive. These patches typically grow 1-3 inches across and have a somewhat bumpy, textured surface that feels slightly rough to the touch. The most distinctive feature is the bright red interior that shows when the small, disk-like fruiting bodies are broken open.

idTips.label: Red interior core
idTips.description: Gently scratch or break open the small, dark fruiting bodies to reveal a brilliant red or crimson interior - this is the diagnostic feature that separates it from other shadow lichens

idTips.label: Crusty gray patches
idTips.description: Forms circular to irregular patches of gray-green crust that feel slightly rough and granular, like fine sandpaper, when you run your finger across them

idTips.label: Small dark discs
idTips.description: Look for tiny, dark brown to black disc-shaped structures (fruiting bodies) scattered across the surface, each about the size of a pinhead

idTips.label: Bark-hugging growth
idTips.description: Grows tightly pressed against tree bark with no raised edges or leafy lobes - it appears painted directly onto the surface

idTips.label: Size and texture
idTips.description: Patches range from coin-sized to palm-sized, with a matte finish that lacks any shiny or glossy appearance

habitat: Found on the bark of deciduous trees, particularly maples, oaks, and ash trees in mixed hardwood forests. Prefers somewhat sheltered locations on tree trunks at eye level or slightly higher, often on the north or east-facing sides where moisture lingers longer. Most commonly spotted in mature forest settings rather than young woodlands or forest edges.

seasonality.spring: Easiest to spot as trees leaf out and bark becomes more visible. The contrast between fresh green leaves and gray lichen patches makes identification simpler.
seasonality.summer: Fruiting bodies are most prominent during humid summer months. The red interior is most vivid when conditions are moist from recent rain.
seasonality.fall: Still visible and identifiable as leaves drop, though the lichen may appear slightly faded. Good time to survey multiple trees as bark becomes more exposed.
seasonality.winter: Remains present and identifiable year-round. Snow cover may make lower trunk specimens hard to access, but eye-level patches stay visible.

funFact: Despite being incredibly rare in New England with only one recorded observation, this lichen can live for decades or even centuries on the same tree, slowly growing outward at a rate of just millimeters per year - meaning that small patch you're looking at could be older than your great-grandparents!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other shadow lichens in the same genus, but the red interior core is the definitive giveaway. Remember: 'Red inside, right ID' - no other shadow lichen in New England has this crimson surprise when you scratch the fruiting bodies.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'endococcinodes' literally means 'red inside,' making this one of the few lichens where the Latin name actually helps with field identification. This species is considered extremely rare in New England, so any sighting would be scientifically valuable and worth reporting to local naturalist groups.
compareHints: Unlike its relatives like Orange-cored Shadow Lichen (which has orange interiors) or Mealy Shadow Lichen (which has white powdery surfaces), Red-cored Starburst Shadow Lichen is the only species in its genus with the distinctive crimson interior. While other shadow lichens may look similar from the outside, none share this dramatic red core feature. The Ciliate Wreath Lichen has tiny hair-like projections along its edges, while this species has smooth, unadorned margins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Phaeophyscia relatives, Orange-cored Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its bright orange pycnidial contents - most other wreath lichens in this genus have white, yellow, or red cores instead.
Among the shadow lichens in its genus, Pom-pom Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its small size and abundant powdery soredia clusters.
Among its wreath lichen relatives, Powder-tipped Shadow Lichen is distinguished by having the white soredia concentrated specifically at the lobe tips rather than scattered across the surface.
Unlike its relatives in the Phaeophyscia genus, Ciliate Wreath Lichen is the only one with prominent white hair-like projections along all lobe edges.
Among its relatives, Hairy Shadow Lichen is distinguished by those characteristic hair-like edge projections that other shadow lichens lack.
Unlike its relatives in the Phaeophyscia genus, Dark Shadow Lichen is easily recognized by its abundant black isidia that cover both the center and edges of the lobes.

Unlike its relatives such as Orange-cored Shadow Lichen (which has orange inner tissues) or Hairy Shadow Lichen (which has fuzzy edges), Mealy Shadow Lichen lacks both colorful internal tissues and hairy margins.
Among its Phaeophyscia relatives, Whiskered Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its particularly prominent marginal cilia and small size.
Among its shadow lichen relatives, Scaly Shadow Lichen is distinguished by its prominently curled, squarrose lobes that create a three-dimensional texture.
